subject: Everyday Science
q: Bats find their way in the dark by:
o: Emitting ultrasound and listening for echoes
explanation: Bats send out high-frequency sounds and judge the position of objects from the returning echoes, a method called echolocation.

subject: Everyday Science
q: SONAR is used by ships mainly to:
o: Locate underwater objects and measure depth using sound waves
explanation: SONAR sends sound pulses through water and times their echoes to find the sea bed, submarines or shoals of fish.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pitch of an ambulance siren seems to rise as it approaches and fall as it moves away. This is due to the:
explanation: Motion of the source squeezes the sound waves ahead of it and stretches those behind, changing the frequency heard by the listener.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Soldiers are ordered to break step while marching across a bridge in order to avoid:
explanation: If the rhythm of marching matches the bridge’s natural frequency, the vibrations can build up dangerously through resonance.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The voltage signal which is generated by microphone is called:
explanation: A microphone produces a voltage that varies continuously in step with the sound wave, which is an analogue signal; it must be sampled to become digital.

subject: Everyday Science
q: During a storm, thunder is heard after the lightning is seen because:
o: Light travels much faster than sound
Thunder is produced after the lightning
Clouds block sound for a while
explanation: Both are produced together, but light arrives almost instantly while sound travels at only about 340 m/s in air.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The speed of light in a vacuum is approximately:
explanation: Light travels about 3 × 10^8 metres, or 300,000 kilometres, every second in a vacuum; nothing travels faster.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A rainbow is formed due to:
o: Absorption of light by water vapour
explanation: Raindrops refract and internally reflect sunlight, and because each colour bends by a different amount, white light is spread into a spectrum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Why does the sky appear blue?
o: Due to the colour of gases in the atmosphere
Due to reflection from the Earth’s surface
Due to absorption of blue light by water vapour
Due to scattering of light in the atmosphere
explanation: Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths of sunlight much more strongly than long (red) ones, so blue light reaches our eyes from all parts of the sky.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Sun appears reddish at sunrise and sunset mainly because:
o: The Sun is cooler in the morning and evening
Clouds reflect red light more strongly
The Earth’s surface gives off red light
Its light passes through a thicker layer of air, which scatters away the blue light
explanation: Near the horizon sunlight travels a long path through the atmosphere, so most blue light is scattered out and mainly red and orange light reaches us.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A pencil partly dipped in a glass of water appears bent at the surface because of:
explanation: Light from the immersed part bends as it passes from water into air, so the pencil appears to be in a different position.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Optical fibres carry light over long distances by the principle of:
explanation: Light striking the inner wall of the fibre at a large angle is reflected completely back inside, so it zigzags along the fibre with little loss.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The appearance of water on a hot desert road (a mirage) is caused by:
o: Reflection of light from the sand
Refraction and total internal reflection of light in layers of hot air
Evaporation of water from the road
explanation: Air near the hot ground is less dense, so light from the sky bends upward until it is totally reflected, appearing to come from a pool on the ground.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Rear-view (side) mirrors in vehicles are:
explanation: Convex mirrors always give an upright, smaller image and a wider field of view, so the driver can see more of the traffic behind.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Shaving and make-up mirrors are usually:
explanation: When the face is close to a concave mirror (within its focal length) the image is upright and magnified.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following lenses is used in the microscope?
explanation: A microscope uses converging (convex) lenses for both the objective and the eyepiece to form a greatly magnified image.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The three primary colours of light are:
explanation: Mixing red, green and blue light in different proportions produces all other colours, and all three together give white; this is how screens work.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A red rose seen in pure green light appears:
explanation: A red object reflects only red light and absorbs other colours; in green light there is no red to reflect, so it looks black.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The waves which are used by the TV remote control are:
explanation: Most TV remotes send coded pulses of invisible infrared light from an LED to a sensor on the television.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Electromagnetic radiation with maximum wavelength is:
explanation: In the electromagnetic spectrum, radio waves have the longest wavelengths (from millimetres to kilometres) and gamma rays the shortest.

subject: Everyday Science
q: X-rays were discovered by:
explanation: Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Beta particles emitted by radioactive substances are:
explanation: Beta radiation consists of high-speed electrons released from the nucleus; alpha particles are helium nuclei and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following radiations can pass through several centimetres of lead?
explanation: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves and are the most penetrating; alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few millimetres of aluminium.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A microwave oven heats food mainly by making which molecules in it vibrate?
explanation: Microwaves make water molecules rotate back and forth rapidly; this motion produces heat throughout the moist food.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Night-vision thermal cameras form images by detecting:
explanation: All warm objects give off infrared radiation, so thermal cameras can “see” people and animals by their heat even in darkness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The word LASER stands for:
o: Light Absorption by Simple Emission of Rays
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Luminous Amplification by Spontaneous Energy Release
Light Accumulation by Stimulated Energy Reflection
explanation: A laser produces an intense, narrow beam of light of a single colour through stimulated emission.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space by:
explanation: Conduction and convection need a medium, but radiation travels as electromagnetic waves and can cross a vacuum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The silvered walls of a vacuum (thermos) flask mainly reduce heat transfer by:
explanation: Shiny silvered surfaces reflect radiant heat back; the vacuum between the walls stops conduction and convection.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cooking pans have handles of wood or plastic because these materials are:
explanation: Wood and plastic are thermal insulators, so the handle stays cool enough to hold while the pan is hot.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Small gaps are left between the rails of a railway track to:
o: Allow the rails to expand in hot weather
explanation: Steel expands when heated; without gaps the rails could buckle on hot days.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Water has its maximum density at a temperature of:
explanation: Unlike most liquids, water contracts on cooling only down to 4 °C; below that it expands again, which is called anomalous expansion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In very cold weather, a lake freezes first at its surface rather than at the bottom because:
o: The bottom is heated by the Sun
Fish keep the lower water warm
Water is densest at 4 °C and ice is lighter than water
explanation: Water cooled below 4 °C becomes lighter and stays on top, and the ice formed floats, insulating the water below so aquatic life survives.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because:
o: The pressure lowers the boiling point of water
The higher pressure raises the boiling point of water
explanation: Trapped steam increases the pressure, so water boils at about 120 °C instead of 100 °C, and the hotter water cooks food faster.

subject: Everyday Science
q: On high mountains water boils at a temperature below 100 °C because:
o: There is less oxygen in the water
explanation: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure; with lower air pressure this happens at a lower temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Water kept in an earthen pot (matka) stays cool in summer because:
o: Water seeping through the pores evaporates and absorbs heat
explanation: Evaporation needs heat, which it takes from the remaining water in the pot, so the water is cooled.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The heat absorbed when ice melts into water without any rise in temperature is called:
explanation: During melting, the added energy breaks the bonds of the solid rather than raising temperature; this hidden energy is the latent heat of fusion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A burn from steam at 100 °C is more severe than one from boiling water at 100 °C because steam:
o: Gives out extra latent heat when it condenses on the skin
Is at a much higher temperature
explanation: On condensing, steam releases its large latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat released as the water cools.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The lowest possible temperature, absolute zero, is approximately:
explanation: Absolute zero (0 K, about −273.15 °C) is the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible energy of motion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Newton’s first law of motion is also known as the law of:
explanation: The first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force, a property called inertia.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The upward motion of a rocket is best explained by Newton’s:
explanation: The rocket pushes hot gases downward (action) and the gases push the rocket upward with an equal and opposite force (reaction).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ball bearings are used in the wheels and moving parts of machines to:
explanation: Rolling balls replace sliding contact with rolling contact, which greatly reduces friction and wear.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The treads on vehicle tyres are designed mainly to:
o: Reduce the weight of the tyre
explanation: Treads increase friction and channel water away from the contact patch, reducing skidding on wet roads.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A person’s weight on the Moon is about ______ of his weight on Earth.
explanation: The Moon’s gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth’s; the person’s mass stays the same but the pull on it is weaker.

subject: Everyday Science
q: If a feather and a stone are dropped together in a vacuum, then:
o: The stone reaches the ground first
The feather reaches the ground first
Both reach the ground at the same time
explanation: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration due to gravity, regardless of mass.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The force that keeps a body moving in a circular path and is directed towards the centre is called:
explanation: Any body moving in a circle needs a net inward (centripetal) force; for a car turning a corner it is supplied by friction on the tyres.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A body immersed in a liquid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces. This is:
explanation: Archimedes’ principle explains why ships float and why objects seem lighter in water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hydraulic brakes and hydraulic lifts work on the basis of:
explanation: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions, so a small force can produce a large one.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The lift on an aeroplane wing is commonly explained using:
explanation: Air flowing faster over the curved upper surface has lower pressure than air below the wing, producing an upward force.

subject: Everyday Science
q: It is easier to swim in sea water than in river water because sea water:
o: Is denser and gives more upthrust
Has waves that push swimmers up
explanation: Dissolved salt makes sea water denser, so it exerts a larger buoyant force on a swimmer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Momentum of a moving body is the product of its:
explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity, so a heavy truck and a fast bullet can both have large momentum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A man stands still holding a heavy suitcase for ten minutes. In the scientific sense, the work he does on the suitcase is:
o: Equal to the weight of the suitcase
explanation: Work is done only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force; the suitcase does not move, so no work is done on it, even though he gets tired.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A stretched bow possesses:
explanation: Energy is stored in the bent bow because of its deformed shape; when released it becomes the kinetic energy of the arrow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: “Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another.” This is the law of:
explanation: The law of conservation of energy says the total energy of an isolated system stays constant during any change.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Small insects such as water striders can walk on water because of:
explanation: Water molecules at the surface pull strongly on each other, forming a thin “skin” that can support very light objects.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Oil rises up the wick of a lamp due to:
explanation: The narrow spaces between the wick’s fibres draw liquid upward because of adhesion between the liquid and the fibres.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Honey flows much more slowly than water because it has a higher:
explanation: Viscosity is a liquid’s resistance to flow; honey’s internal friction is far greater than that of water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (1921) chiefly for his explanation of the:
explanation: The Nobel committee cited his law of the photoelectric effect, which showed that light behaves as packets of energy; relativity was not the stated reason.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of force is the:
explanation: One newton is the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of work and energy is the:
explanation: One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of power is the:
explanation: Power is the rate of doing work; one watt means one joule of energy transferred every second.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of pressure is the:
explanation: One pascal is a force of one newton acting on an area of one square metre; the bar and atmosphere are non-SI units.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of electric current is the:
explanation: The ampere is one of the seven SI base units and measures the rate of flow of electric charge.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Electrical resistance is measured in:
explanation: The ohm, named after Georg Ohm, is the resistance through which one volt drives a current of one ampere.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Potential difference (voltage) is measured in:
explanation: The volt, named after Alessandro Volta, measures the energy given to each unit of charge in a circuit.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of electric charge is the:
explanation: One coulomb is the charge carried by a current of one ampere flowing for one second.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Frequency is measured in:
explanation: One hertz means one complete cycle or vibration per second.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI base unit of temperature is the:
explanation: The kelvin is the SI base unit; its scale starts at absolute zero, and a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI base unit of mass is the:
explanation: The kilogram is the only SI base unit with a prefix in its name; the newton measures force (weight), not mass.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI base unit of luminous intensity is the:
explanation: The candela measures how bright a light source is in a particular direction; lux and lumen are derived units for illumination and light output.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many base units are there in the International System of Units (SI)?
explanation: The seven SI base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela; all other units are derived from them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The SI unit of magnetic flux density (magnetic field strength) is the:
explanation: The tesla, named after Nikola Tesla, measures the strength of a magnetic field; the henry measures inductance and the farad capacitance.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kilowatt-hour (the “unit” on an electricity bill) is a unit of:
explanation: A kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1,000-watt appliance running for one hour, so it measures energy, not power.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Horsepower is a unit of:
explanation: Horsepower, still used for engines and motors, measures the rate of doing work; one horsepower is about 746 watts.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A light-year is a unit of:
explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres; it is used for distances to stars.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance between the:
explanation: The astronomical unit, about 150 million kilometres, is the mean Earth–Sun distance and is used for distances within the solar system.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The parsec is a unit used in astronomy to measure:
explanation: One parsec is about 3.26 light-years; it is based on the apparent shift (parallax) of a star as the Earth orbits the Sun.
